note: The ABA's Routing Number Policy (revised 9/20, read 2026-10-30 on aba.com) gives the routing number as nine digits: a four-digit Federal Reserve Routing Symbol (01-12 for banks, by Federal Reserve district), a four-digit ABA institution identifier (the page misprints it 'Intuition') and a check digit; the ABA's own page puts the account number right after it on a cheque. The check digit is the one the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's Circular No. 8203 (19 October 1977, read 2026-10-30 in the St. Louis Fed's FRASER copy) announced for the joint ABA/Federal Reserve programme in force from 1 July 1978: 'a Modulus-10, weights 3, 7, 1, check digit as the last digit in the Routing Number field'. The weights are read left to right over the first eight digits (3, 7, 1, 3, 7, 1, 3, 7), the check digit being what brings the sum to a multiple of ten; that reading was checked on the page of the Key to Routing Numbers enclosed with the circular, whose 0219-0757 (7), 0213-0763 (0) and 0219-0797 (5) all pass it, and on Bank of Guam's routing number 121405115 (its own page, read 2026-10-30). No national standard fixes the account number's length: the Fiscal Service's Green Book says only that account numbers may be up to 17 characters, letters or digits. JPMorgan Chase, the largest bank, says a checking account number is often eight to 12 digits long and gives no single length in text; so the account number is held as the Green Book gives it, one to seventeen characters, and a new one is drawn at eight to twelve digits, as Chase says its own are. (Until 2026-10-30 this file held nine digits, counted from the placeholder zeros of the sample check on Chase's routing-numbers page; a picture's placeholders aren't a length the bank states, and the lead held the file back.) A whole worked number (routing and account together) isn't published by any source read, so the form has no example. The routing number is held as the bank's code (characters 1 to 8, the check digit worked from them). NACHA's ACH developer guide answered with a Cloudflare challenge and wasn't read; the Federal Reserve's E-Payments Routing Directory pages sit behind a terms-of-use agreement and weren't entered.
